case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court may invoke judicial estoppel to bar a bankruptcy debtor’s later civil tort claim based solely on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim’s underlying facts and a motive to conceal it, or whether New Hampshire v. Maine requires a holistic, circumstance-specific inquiry (including bad faith/intent) before estoppel applies.
case_analysis.legal_provision: No single statute directly governs judicial estoppel; the dispute arises at the intersection of the federal common-law doctrine of judicial estoppel (as articulated in New Hampshire v. Maine) and the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure and estate-administration framework (e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 (debtor’s disclosure duties) and 541 (property of the estate)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues that the Fifth Circuit applied an overly rigid, near-automatic judicial-estoppel rule that treats nondisclosure as non-inadvertent whenever the debtor knew the facts and had a motive to conceal, contrary to New Hampshire v. Maine’s equitable, multi-factor approach. He contends courts must assess the full context—including the debtor’s actual intent, the bankruptcy case’s posture, steps taken to correct omissions, and whether creditors/trustee can be protected—rather than imposing a categorical bar that can unfairly punish creditors and over-deter legitimate claims.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues that judicial estoppel can bar an undisclosed civil claim regardless of direct evidence of subjective bad faith, because the integrity of the bankruptcy system depends on complete disclosure and debtors almost always have a motive to conceal assets. It emphasizes that Keathley repeatedly omitted known, pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims from his schedules and disclosed only after the defendant moved for summary judgment, supporting estoppel to prevent a debtor from taking inconsistent positions and to deter strategic nondisclosure.
key_precedents: New Hampshire v. Maine (judicial estoppel factors and equitable nature of the doctrine)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly emphasize that bankruptcy depends on strict, continuing disclosure under §§ 521 and 541, and that courts may draw reasonable inferences from objective conduct without a freestanding subjective-intent requirement. But their “knowledge + motive” approach, as Justice Kagan underscores, risks hardening New Hampshire v. Maine’s equitable, nonexhaustive guideposts into a near-automatic rule in the run of bankruptcy cases where “motive” is ubiquitous, thereby departing from the circumstance-specific inquiry our precedent demands. I also agree with Justice Barrett that creditor-protection concerns are not merely remedial afterthoughts: an automatic estoppel bar can destroy estate value that the trustee could administer once the omission is corrected, even though bankruptcy courts already possess targeted tools (reopening, amendments, sanctions) to address nondisclosure. The narrower, precedent-faithful course is to require a totality-of-circumstances application of New Hampshire—allowing strong inferences from timing and “caught-only” corrections, as Justice Alito notes, but rejecting any quasi-categorical presumption untethered from the holistic inquiry.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s reliance on New Hampshire v. Maine, echoed by Justices Barrett and Gorsuch, correctly describes judicial estoppel as equitable and guided by nonexclusive factors, but it does not establish a requirement of a free-ranging “totality” inquiry that effectively disables courts from drawing strong objective inferences in bankruptcy. Where a debtor had a clear, continuing statutory duty to disclose under §§ 521 and 541 and nevertheless obtained the benefits of the bankruptcy process while omitting a known claim, the integrity-of-the-courts concern New Hampshire identifies is triggered without needing a subjective-intent mini-trial. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan’s creditor-harm point is best handled by limiting estoppel’s operation to the debtor (allowing trustee substitution), not by weakening the estoppel rule in a way that invites strategic nondisclosure. Under my methodology, nothing in New Hampshire’s text compels converting this doctrine into an amorphous, case-by-case balancing test that tolerates objectively inconsistent positions when the bankruptcy court has been asked to act on incomplete disclosures.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s point that New Hampshire v. Maine requires a flexible, circumstance-specific inquiry is the strongest objection to the Fifth Circuit’s articulation, but I do not read New Hampshire to forbid drawing robust, practical inferences from objective bankruptcy facts—especially the Code’s continuing disclosure duty under §§ 521 and 541 and a debtor’s correction only after being caught. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right that an overbroad estoppel rule can reduce recoveries for creditors, yet that concern goes to tailoring the remedy (e.g., allowing the trustee to proceed) rather than weakening estoppel’s deterrent function against strategic nondisclosure by the debtor. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern is overstated because judicial estoppel is a narrow, longstanding equitable doctrine aimed at protecting courts from being misled, and applying it in bankruptcy where nondisclosure predictably distorts the process fits squarely within New Hampshire’s guideposts. On a consequence-sensitive textualist view, an approach that treats knowledge and motive as strong evidence—rebuttable in truly inadvertent cases—better preserves the integrity of the bankruptcy system than the petitioner’s more permissive standard.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: bankruptcy’s disclosure regime under §§ 521 and 541 is unusually stringent, and an objective inference can deter “fast and loose” omissions without litigating subjective intent. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, New Hampshire v. Maine characterizes judicial estoppel as equitable “guideposts” applied to specific contexts, and converting ubiquitous “knowledge + motive” into a near-dispositive presumption effectively hardens equity into strict liability—often wiping out estate value that should flow to creditors. I’m persuaded that we can protect integrity without automatic forfeiture by requiring a holistic inquiry into whether the bankruptcy court actually adopted the debtor’s position, whether any unfair advantage was realized, and whether the omission was promptly cured—while still allowing strong inferences of bad faith from timing and conduct (including “corrected only after being caught,” as Justice Alito notes). Given the Code’s built-in tools (reopening, amendment, trustee substitution, sanctions), an overbroad federal common-law estoppel rule is unnecessary and risks disproportionate harm to vulnerable debtors and innocent creditors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas have the strongest point that §§ 521 and 541 impose a stringent, continuing disclosure regime, and that post-discharge "corrections" only after being caught can justify powerful inferences of manipulation. But that goes to what facts warrant estoppel, not to converting New Hampshire v. Maine’s equitable, nonexhaustive guideposts into a near-dispositive "knowledge + motive" presumption—especially when motive is endemic in bankruptcy and would effectively collapse the inadvertence/timely-cure inquiry. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, an automatic estoppel bar can perversely destroy estate value the trustee could administer for creditors, undercutting both the Bankruptcy Code’s structure and the integrity rationale estoppel purports to serve. My approach keeps robust deterrence by allowing courts to infer bad faith from timing and conduct (as Alito notes), while still requiring the context-sensitive New Hampshire inquiry rather than treating knowledge+motive as dispositive.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly emphasize that §§ 521 and 541 impose a stringent, continuing disclosure duty and that nondisclosure threatens the integrity of the bankruptcy process; those statutory tools, plus sanctions and trustee control, already address concealment without our enlarging federal common law. But their proposed “knowledge + motive” inference risks becoming quasi-categorical in ordinary bankruptcies where motive is ubiquitous, effectively converting New Hampshire v. Maine’s nonexclusive, context-specific guideposts into a near-presumption untethered from the holistic inquiry that precedent demands. As the Chief Justice notes, an automatic estoppel bar can also destroy estate value that the trustee could administer for creditors, which cuts against the Code’s design and counsels restraint under separation-of-powers principles. I would thus hold courts must apply New Hampshire’s totality-of-circumstances framework—permitting strong inferences from timing and conduct (as Justice Alito suggests) but rejecting a rigid rule that makes knowledge+motive effectively dispositive.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito offer the strongest point that bankruptcy’s disclosure duties under §§ 521 and 541 are unusually clear and that courts may infer manipulation from objective circumstances without a subjective-intent mini-trial. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as flexible equity guided by nonexclusive factors, and treating “knowledge + motive” (often ubiquitous in bankruptcy) as near-dispositive risks converting that precedent into an effectively categorical rule untethered from the holistic inquiry we required. I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett that this rigidity can perversely destroy estate value that the trustee could otherwise administer for creditors, while bankruptcy courts retain tailored tools (reopening, amendment, sanctions, trustee substitution) to address nondisclosure case-specifically. The proper path is to insist on a totality-of-circumstances application of New Hampshire—allowing strong inferences of bad faith from timing and conduct, but not a quasi-automatic estoppel bar based solely on knowledge and a generalized motive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that bankruptcy’s strict disclosure regime under §§ 521 and 541 makes strategic omission both predictable and corrosive, so courts should be able to infer manipulation from objective facts without an intent mini-trial. But New Hampshire v. Maine deliberately framed judicial estoppel as equitable “guideposts” applied in specific factual contexts, and Justice Roberts is right that converting “knowledge + motive” (nearly always present) into a near-dispositive presumption effectively rewrites that flexible standard into a categorical rule. Even accepting Justice Thomas’s emphasis that undisclosed claims remain estate property, that statutory consequence already protects creditors and supplies remedies, which counsels restraint in expanding a judge-made doctrine into something like strict liability. A totality approach can still draw strong inferences from timing (e.g., correction only after being caught) while preserving New Hampshire’s methodological instruction and avoiding needless destruction of estate value.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right that §§ 521 and 541 impose a stringent, continuing duty of disclosure, and that repeated omissions can justify strong inferences that protect bankruptcy’s integrity. But Chief Justice Roberts (echoed by Justices Kagan and Sotomayor) correctly emphasizes that New Hampshire v. Maine treats judicial estoppel as “strong medicine” governed by nonexclusive, context-specific factors—not a near-dispositive knowledge+motive presumption that effectively eliminates the debtor’s opportunity to show inadvertence or timely cure. On my procedural-fairness, consequence-aware approach, the equitable inquiry must remain holistic: courts may infer bad faith from objective timing and conduct (including “only after being caught”), but they must still assess adoption, unfair advantage, and the availability of tailored remedies that preserve estate value for creditors. That preserves deterrence while avoiding disproportionate forfeiture that can punish creditors and collapse equity into quasi-strict liability.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, circumstance-specific doctrine guided by nonexhaustive factors (including inconsistency, risk of unfair advantage, and related considerations), not a near-categorical presumption triggered by mere “knowledge + motive,” which would effectively make estoppel automatic in most bankruptcies. A rigid rule also risks harming the Bankruptcy Code’s core aims by unnecessarily extinguishing estate value that should in the first instance be administered for creditors under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541, and it intrudes on the bankruptcy court’s ability to police disclosures through its own remedies. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and narrow decisionmaking, I would hold only that courts must undertake the holistic New Hampshire inquiry—considering the full context (including whether the omission was inadvertent or corrected and whether any unfair advantage would result)—before applying judicial estoppel in this setting. That approach respects precedent, avoids overbroad federal common-law rules, and preserves room for case-specific sanctions where intentional concealment is shown.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine, but nothing in New Hampshire v. Maine requires courts to engage in a free-ranging inquiry into subjective intent as a prerequisite to estoppel; the doctrine’s core concern is protecting the integrity of the judicial process when a litigant takes inconsistent positions. In the bankruptcy context, the Bankruptcy Code imposes affirmative, continuing disclosure duties on debtors, see 11 U.S.C. § 521, and undisclosed causes of action are property of the estate, see 11 U.S.C. § 541; permitting a debtor to pursue an omitted tort claim after obtaining bankruptcy relief undermines the system’s reliance on candid schedules. Where, as here, the debtor knew the underlying facts and had a clear incentive to conceal a potential asset while the bankruptcy case proceeded, an objective estoppel rule is consistent with the equitable purpose identified in New Hampshire and serves to deter manipulation without expanding federal judicial power beyond its proper bounds. Accordingly, I would affirm the application of judicial estoppel on these facts rather than impose a mandatory intent-based inquiry.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, federal common-law doctrine aimed at protecting the integrity of the judicial process, and New Hampshire v. Maine makes clear that courts may apply it using practical “guideposts” rather than a rigid checklist, especially where a party advances inconsistent positions and gains (or seeks to gain) an unfair advantage. In the bankruptcy setting, the Bankruptcy Code imposes a clear, continuing duty of full disclosure, see 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541, and allowing a debtor to pursue an undisclosed tort claim after omitting it from schedules undermines that disclosure regime and invites strategic nondisclosure with predictable practical consequences for trustees and creditors. Where, as alleged here, the debtor repeatedly failed to disclose known claims and only corrected after the opposing party raised estoppel, a court may infer that the omission was not inadvertent and invoke estoppel without requiring direct proof of subjective bad faith. This approach deters “fast and loose” litigation tactics, preserves the bankruptcy system’s reliability, and aligns with New Hampshire’s emphasis on preventing abuse and protecting judicial integrity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine requires a circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a near-automatic rule triggered by mere knowledge of underlying facts plus a generic “motive to conceal.” In the bankruptcy context—where 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 already supply disclosure and estate-protection mechanisms—a rigid estoppel rule can inflict collateral harm on creditors and vulnerable debtors by forfeiting potentially valuable causes of action without asking whether the omission was actually intentional or whether the trustee can administer the claim for the estate. Consistent with New Hampshire, courts should assess factors such as inconsistency, whether the bankruptcy court accepted the earlier position, and whether the omission resulted from “inadvertence or mistake,” with attention to the debtor’s intent and corrective steps taken. Because the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively presumes bad faith from knowledge and incentive alone, it departs from the equitable, holistic framework this Court articulated and risks inequitable real-world outcomes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine characterizes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine and offers non-exhaustive factors, cautioning that application "will likely depend on specific factual contexts" rather than categorical rules. A near-automatic bankruptcy presumption (knowledge of facts + motive to conceal) risks collapsing that holistic inquiry into a rigid bar, untethered to whether the debtor in fact intended to mislead the bankruptcy court or whether the omission was corrected in time to protect the estate and creditors, contrary to the doctrine’s purpose of safeguarding judicial integrity. The Bankruptcy Code already supplies disclosure and administration mechanisms—e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541—to capture undisclosed claims for the estate; an intent-insensitive estoppel rule can perversely punish creditors by eliminating value that should flow to the estate. A circumstance-specific approach better harmonizes New Hampshire’s equitable framework with bankruptcy workability by permitting estoppel where the record shows manipulation, while allowing remedies that preserve estate value when the omission was inadvertent or promptly cured.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, judge-made doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine makes clear it is not reducible to rigid, categorical rules but instead turns on a circumstance-specific inquiry aimed at protecting the integrity of the judicial process. A near-automatic presumption of bad faith from mere knowledge of underlying facts plus a generic “motive to conceal” (common to most debtors) risks converting equity into strict liability and displacing the Bankruptcy Code’s own mechanisms for addressing nondisclosure, including administration of estate property under 11 U.S.C. § 541 and the debtor’s disclosure duties under § 521. Separation-of-powers principles counsel caution before federal courts expand a common-law preclusion doctrine to impose an irrebuttable presumption untethered from New Hampshire’s holistic factors, especially where such a rule may harm creditors the Code seeks to protect. Consistent with New Hampshire, courts should consider the full context—including whether the debtor acted in bad faith/intent and whether omissions were corrected—before invoking this “strong medicine.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, judge-made doctrine that New Hampshire v. Maine describes as requiring a flexible, circumstance-specific inquiry guided by non-exhaustive factors, not a near-automatic rule. A categorical Fifth Circuit approach that deems nondisclosure “non-inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew the underlying facts and had a theoretical motive to conceal effectively collapses the equitable analysis and risks sweeping in negligent or correctable omissions, contrary to New Hampshire’s emphasis on protecting the judicial process through a holistic assessment (including whether the party acted intentionally and whether the court was misled). In the bankruptcy context, the Code already imposes disclosure duties (11 U.S.C. § 521) and defines estate property (11 U.S.C. § 541), and a rigid estoppel rule can impair practical workability by punishing creditors and trustees who may be able to administer the claim for the estate if the omission is cured. Consistent with judicial restraint and precedent, I would require lower courts to apply New Hampshire’s totality-of-circumstances framework—intent and corrective steps included—rather than treating knowledge-plus-motive as dispositive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine describes it as a flexible, factor-based inquiry rather than a mechanical rule; a near-automatic bar based solely on “knowledge of facts + motive” collapses the doctrine into an irrebuttable presumption and departs from that precedent’s circumstance-specific approach. The Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) supplies strong reasons to police nondisclosure, but it does not itself mandate forfeiture of the estate’s claim; courts must still apply estoppel consistently with its equitable nature and consider context, including whether the debtor acted in bad faith and whether corrective steps can protect the trustee and creditors. Treating the “inadvertence” consideration in New Hampshire as dispositive—and defining it categorically—fails methodological consistency with this Court’s instruction that estoppel turns on multiple considerations (including unfair advantage) evaluated holistically. I would therefore vacate the Fifth Circuit’s rigid rule and require a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry before estoppel may bar the tort claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine characterizes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine requiring a holistic, circumstance-specific inquiry, not a near-automatic bar triggered solely by knowledge of underlying facts and a generalized “motive” to conceal. The Fifth Circuit’s rigid knowledge-and-motive presumption effectively collapses the bad-faith/intent analysis and risks unfair practical consequences in bankruptcy—foreclosing potentially meritorious claims and harming creditors and the estate that 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 are designed to protect. Consistent with Maine’s flexible factors (including whether the prior position was adopted by the court and whether estoppel is necessary to prevent unfair advantage), courts should evaluate intent, the bankruptcy posture, and corrective steps (e.g., reopening/amending schedules) before applying estoppel. Procedural fairness requires giving the debtor an opportunity to be heard on intent and tailoring any remedy to safeguard creditors without imposing a categorical forfeiture.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court may invoke judicial estoppel to bar a debtor’s undisclosed civil claim based only on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a motive to conceal it, or whether New Hampshire v. Maine requires a holistic, circumstance-specific inquiry (including bad faith/intent) before estoppel applies.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal common-law doctrine of judicial estoppel as applied in the bankruptcy context (interacting with the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure and estate-administration scheme, e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541, and related schedules/disclosure obligations).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues the Fifth Circuit misapplied New Hampshire v. Maine by treating nondisclosure as non-inadvertent (and thus estoppel-worthy) essentially per se whenever a debtor knew of the claim and had a motive to conceal it. He contends judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine that must be applied flexibly, requiring a holistic assessment of intent and all circumstances, not a rigid inference of bad faith from knowledge-plus-motive alone. He also emphasizes that an overly automatic estoppel rule undermines bankruptcy’s goals by harming creditors (who could benefit from the claim) and by allowing civil defendants an undeserved windfall unrelated to protecting judicial integrity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues judicial estoppel properly bars Keathley’s personal-injury suit because he repeatedly and deliberately failed to disclose pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims in his bankruptcy schedules, only disclosing after the defendant moved for summary judgment based on nondisclosure. Respondent maintains that courts may apply estoppel regardless of direct evidence of subjective bad faith because nondisclosure of a known claim in bankruptcy is inherently inconsistent with later pursuing it, and permitting the suit would reward concealment, undermine the integrity of the bankruptcy process, and incentivize strategic nondisclosure.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence point—that bankruptcy depends on candor and that “knowledge plus incentive,” especially with correction only after being challenged, is powerful evidence of manipulation—is the strongest case for Respondent, and New Hampshire v. Maine certainly allows courts to draw commonsense inferences from objective facts. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, New Hampshire also insists judicial estoppel remains an equitable, non-mechanical doctrine preserving room for “inadvertence or mistake,” and a rule that makes knowledge-and-motive effectively dispositive risks collapsing that flexibility into a near-irrebuttable presumption. Justice Thomas is right that New Hampshire’s factors are nonexhaustive, yet that does not license reading discretion out of the doctrine—particularly where an estoppel bar can divert value from the estate and innocent creditors to civil defendants, conflicting with the Code’s creditor-protective structure under §§ 521 and 541. The narrower, legitimacy-preserving holding is to require a genuine totality-of-circumstances inquiry in which knowledge and motive are probative but not outcome-determinative, with attention to corrective steps and the trustee/estate’s interests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that New Hampshire v. Maine warns against mechanical application and preserves room for “inadvertence or mistake,” and I agree the doctrine cannot be reduced to an irrebuttable presumption. But nothing in New Hampshire’s text forbids a court, acting in equity, from treating objective facts—knowledge of the claim, a concrete incentive to conceal it from the estate, and correction only after being challenged—as powerful evidence of non-inadvertence, especially given the Bankruptcy Code’s affirmative disclosure duties in §§ 521 and 541. The “windfall to civil defendants” concern highlighted by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan is a policy objection that cannot override equity’s core function of protecting the integrity of judicial proceedings; courts retain discretion to tailor relief (including trustee substitution) where the estate’s interests truly require it, but they need not disable estoppel when the record supports deliberate self-contradiction. Because the Fifth Circuit’s approach can be read as an inference-based application of New Hampshire’s flexible factors rather than a categorical rule, I do not see a legal argument here that undermines affirmance on original equitable terms.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s warning that New Hampshire v. Maine resists mechanical rules is the most serious objection, and I agree knowledge-plus-incentive cannot be treated as an irrebuttable presumption in every case. But on this record—repeated nondisclosure, a clear personal benefit from concealment, and correction only after being confronted (as Justice Thomas emphasizes)—the Fifth Circuit’s inference of non-inadvertence fits comfortably within New Hampshire’s flexible, equity-guided factors rather than replacing them. Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to worry about creditor harm and defendant windfalls, yet that concern goes to tailoring the equitable remedy (e.g., trustee substitution, reopening, limiting estoppel to the debtor’s personal recovery) rather than disabling estoppel’s core function of protecting the integrity of the bankruptcy process. Under a practical, consequence-aware textualism, the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure duties (§ 521) and estate ownership rules (§ 541) reinforce that a debtor’s omission of a known claim is materially inconsistent and may properly support estoppel when the surrounding facts show strategic manipulation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the best point for Respondent: bankruptcy’s disclosure regime depends on candor, and repeated nondisclosure plus late correction can be powerful objective evidence of manipulation. But even on their account, New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as a discretionary equitable doctrine that preserves “inadvertence or mistake,” and a Fifth Circuit-style knowledge-plus-incentive shortcut risks functioning as an almost irrebuttable presumption in the very class of cases where those two facts will frequently be present. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that rigidity can produce windfalls for civil defendants and impair creditor recovery—outcomes misaligned with the Bankruptcy Code’s estate-centric structure under §§ 521 and 541 and with equity’s aim of protecting judicial integrity rather than imposing forfeiture. Knowledge and motive should remain probative, but courts must examine the full record (timing, counsel’s role, corrective steps, and trustee substitution/reopening) before applying the harsh sanction of estoppel.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence-and-administrability point is the strongest for Respondent, and I agree that knowledge of a claim plus a concrete incentive to conceal can be powerful evidence of bad faith in bankruptcy. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine characterizes judicial estoppel as flexible equity and expressly preserves space for “inadvertence or mistake,” and a knowledge-plus-motive approach that effectively becomes dispositive collapses that textual flexibility into a near-per-se rule. Justice Thomas is right that New Hampshire’s factors are nonexhaustive and do not “constitutionalize” a checklist, yet that does not license converting two common features of many omissions into an irrebuttable proxy for intent—especially when the Bankruptcy Code’s structure under §§ 521 and 541 means an automatic estoppel often strips value from the estate and creditors while handing a windfall to the civil defendant. The more coherent, workable rule is a genuine totality-of-circumstances inquiry in which knowledge and motive remain probative, with remedies calibrated to protect judicial integrity without gratuitous forfeiture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right that bankruptcy’s disclosure duties under §§ 521 and 541 are stringent and that “knowledge plus incentive,” especially coupled with correction only after being challenged, is powerful evidence of manipulation. But even accepting that evidentiary force, New Hampshire v. Maine treats judicial estoppel as discretionary equity that must leave meaningful room for “inadvertence or mistake,” and a Fifth Circuit-style approach that makes knowledge-and-motive effectively dispositive converts a permissible inference into a near-irrebuttable presumption. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, that rigidity risks producing windfalls for civil defendants while impairing the Code’s creditor-protective design—an outcome hard to justify on textualist/originalist grounds where Congress has supplied specific bankruptcy remedies for nondisclosure. Courts may infer bad faith from the whole record, but they must actually weigh the circumstances rather than apply a shortcut that functionally extinguishes estate value by rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point—that bankruptcy needs a strong deterrent and that “knowledge plus incentive” is objective evidence of manipulation—has real force, and I agree those facts may support an inference of bad faith. But as the Chief Justice stresses, New Hampshire v. Maine warns against turning judicial estoppel into a mechanical rule and expressly preserves “inadvertence or mistake”; a framework that treats two features present in most nondisclosures (knowledge and generic motive) as essentially dispositive risks functionally eliminating that carve-out. Justice Thomas is right that New Hampshire’s factors are nonexhaustive, yet that discretion cuts against a near-per-se inference that strips equity of its circumstance-specific character—especially where the Bankruptcy Code’s structure (§§ 521, 541) and tools like reopening/amendment and trustee control mean an automatic estoppel bar can produce a windfall for the civil defendant while harming creditors. I therefore remain with Petitioner: knowledge and incentive are probative, but courts must consider the full record (including corrective steps and estate interests) before imposing the harsh sanction of estoppel.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas make the strongest point that bankruptcy’s disclosure duties are central and that knowledge plus an incentive to conceal can be powerful objective evidence of manipulation, particularly where correction comes only after being challenged. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine with nonexclusive factors and an express safety valve for “inadvertence or mistake,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-and-motive approach risks operating as a de facto conclusive presumption that drains that caveat of meaning. Textually, the Bankruptcy Code already specifies consequences and mechanisms for nondisclosure and estate control of claims (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541), so an automatic estoppel that extinguishes value can misalign with the Code’s creditor-protective structure and produce the windfall Justice Kagan flags. Consistent with original equitable principles and our precedent, knowledge and motive should remain probative—often strongly so—but the court must still assess the full record (including amendment/reopening and trustee substitution) before imposing the harsh, integrity-protecting sanction of estoppel.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence-and-administrability argument is the strongest for Respondent: bankruptcy relies on debtor candor, and repeated nondisclosure plus correction only after challenge can be powerful evidence of manipulation. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as flexible equity and explicitly preserves room for “inadvertence or mistake,” so treating “knowledge plus incentive” as effectively dispositive risks converting a probative inference into a near-irrebuttable presumption. Justice Thomas is right that New Hampshire did not constitutionalize a rigid multi-factor checklist, yet that same flexibility cuts against adopting the Fifth Circuit’s shortcut as a de facto rule—especially where the Bankruptcy Code’s mechanisms (reopening/amendment and trustee control of estate claims) can protect judicial integrity and creditors without conferring a windfall on civil defendants. On my pragmatic, fairness-focused view, courts should require a genuine totality-of-the-circumstances finding of bad faith and reliance before imposing the harsh sanction of estoppel.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, circumstance-specific doctrine and cautions against rigid, per se applications, including where the prior position resulted from “inadvertence or mistake.” A rule effectively presuming bad faith from knowledge of a claim plus a generic “motive to conceal” risks turning that flexible inquiry into an almost automatic forfeiture, which is difficult to reconcile with New Hampshire’s holistic approach and threatens institutional legitimacy by producing windfalls for civil defendants unrelated to protecting judicial integrity. In the bankruptcy context, the disclosure scheme in 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 is principally administered to protect the estate and creditors; a categorical estoppel rule can impair that federal framework by extinguishing assets that could inure to the estate rather than tailoring relief to misconduct. The narrower, precedent-faithful course is to require courts to consider all relevant circumstances (including the debtor’s explanation and corrective disclosures) before applying estoppel, rather than treating knowledge-and-motive as dispositive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law equitable doctrine aimed at protecting the integrity of the judicial process, and New Hampshire v. Maine emphasizes preventing “intentional self-contradiction … as a means of obtaining unfair advantage,” while also recognizing an exception for “inadvertence or mistake.” In the bankruptcy context, the Code imposes affirmative, continuing disclosure obligations (e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541), and a debtor’s pursuit of a civil claim after omitting it from schedules presents the kind of inconsistent position that undermines the bankruptcy court’s administration of the estate. Given that New Hampshire does not constitutionalize a rigid, multi-factor test, I would not read it to forbid lower courts from inferring deliberateness from objective circumstances such as knowledge of the claim and a concrete incentive to omit it, particularly where the debtor corrected only after being confronted. Accordingly, the Fifth Circuit’s approach, as applied to repeated nondisclosure, falls within the permissible exercise of equitable discretion to deter manipulation of the bankruptcy system.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine aimed at preventing “the perversion of the judicial process,” and it endorses flexible factors—including whether a party’s later position is “clearly inconsistent” and whether the party would gain an unfair advantage. In the bankruptcy setting, the Code’s disclosure regime (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) makes a debtor’s omission of a known claim from schedules fundamentally inconsistent with later pursuing that claim for personal benefit, and knowledge plus a concrete incentive to conceal ordinarily supports an inference of non-inadvertence. Requiring a searching, subjective bad-faith inquiry in every case would undermine practical administration of bankruptcy, invite strategic nondisclosure, and impair the integrity of the process that depends on complete debtor candor. Given the repeated nondisclosures and the late correction only after summary-judgment pressure, applying estoppel here is a permissible exercise of equitable discretion under New Hampshire’s framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine “not reducible to any general formulation,” requiring a circumstance-specific balancing aimed at protecting judicial integrity rather than imposing a near-automatic bar. A knowledge-plus-motive presumption in bankruptcy nondisclosure cases is too rigid and risks inequitable results, including harming innocent creditors who, under 11 U.S.C. §§ 541 and 521, are the true beneficiaries of estate assets and depend on accurate administration rather than forfeiture windfalls to civil defendants. Courts should therefore examine the full record—including the debtor’s intent, the role of counsel, timing of correction, and remedial alternatives (e.g., reopening, substitution of trustee)—before applying estoppel. That holistic approach better serves fairness and the real-world administration of bankruptcy while still allowing estoppel where the circumstances show deliberate manipulation of the courts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, flexible doctrine guided by several nonexclusive factors—not a mechanical rule—and it specifically contemplates that courts may decline estoppel where the earlier position resulted from “inadvertence or mistake.” In the bankruptcy setting, collapsing that inquiry into a near-per-se inference of bad faith from “knowledge of the claim plus motive to conceal” risks overdeterrence and poor fit with the Bankruptcy Code’s administration scheme (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541), because the real party in interest is often the estate and creditors may be harmed by forfeiture of value. A circumstance-specific inquiry better serves the doctrine’s core purpose—protecting judicial integrity—while allowing tailored remedies (e.g., reopening, substitution of the trustee) when nondisclosure is negligent rather than strategic. The Fifth Circuit’s approach reads New Hampshire v. Maine’s flexible factors as a rigid intent proxy, and that lack of workability and statutory coherence counsels against it.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine applied “at [the court’s] discretion,” guided by nonexhaustive factors and sensitive to “inadvertence or mistake,” 532 U.S. 742, 750–753 (2001). A per se rule that deems nondisclosure “not inadvertent” whenever a debtor had knowledge and a theoretical motive to conceal improperly converts a circumstance-specific equitable inquiry into a rigid presumption, untethered from New Hampshire’s holistic framework. In the bankruptcy setting, the Code already supplies tools to address nondisclosure (e.g., the debtor’s disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. § 521 and the estate’s ownership of claims under § 541), and an automatic estoppel that bars the claim outright risks awarding civil defendants a windfall while frustrating administration for creditors—results hard to reconcile with a disciplined separation-of-powers approach to judge-made doctrines. Courts may still estop in appropriate cases, but New Hampshire requires attention to the full context (including whether the omission was truly mistaken or strategically calculated) rather than a knowledge-plus-motive shortcut.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, non-mechanical doctrine guided by non-exhaustive factors and cautions against application that would effectively punish “inadvertence or mistake,” which cuts against a per se rule triggered solely by knowledge plus motive. In the bankruptcy context, the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) can be enforced through Code remedies (including amendment, trustee administration of estate property, and potential sanctions), and an automatic estoppel rule risks practical unworkability by producing windfalls for civil defendants at the expense of creditors—undermining the system’s integrity the doctrine is meant to protect. A circumstance-specific inquiry into intent/bad faith better aligns with history and precedent, preserves equitable discretion, and avoids converting judicial estoppel into a rigid punitive rule. Under judicial restraint, the Court should require lower courts to apply New Hampshire’s holistic framework rather than infer bad faith categorically from knowledge and theoretical motive alone.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine guided by nonexhaustive factors and cautions against rigid application, including refusing to punish "inadvertence or mistake"; that framework does not support a near-per-se rule that infers bad faith solely from a debtor’s knowledge of a claim plus a generalized motive to conceal. Textually and structurally, the Bankruptcy Code assigns disclosure and estate-administration consequences to nondisclosure (e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541), and an automatic estoppel bar risks reallocating value from the estate and creditors to civil defendants without the circumstance-specific inquiry equity requires. Consistent with Maine’s focus on protecting judicial integrity, a court may consider knowledge and motive as probative, but must assess the totality of circumstances—including intent/bad faith and remedial steps (e.g., amendment, reopening, trustee action)—before invoking the harsh sanction of estoppel. Because the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively collapses the intent inquiry into an irrebuttable presumption, it is methodologically inconsistent with Maine’s original public meaning and the doctrine’s equitable nature.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as an equitable, circumstance-specific doctrine that turns on multiple factors—most centrally whether the party’s later position is clearly inconsistent, whether the earlier court accepted the prior position, and whether the change would create an unfair advantage—rather than a near-per-se rule triggered by “knowledge plus motive.” In the bankruptcy context, §§ 521 and 541 create robust disclosure and estate-administration tools (including reopening, amendment of schedules, and trustee control of estate claims) that can protect judicial integrity and creditors without automatically extinguishing potentially valuable claims for the benefit of civil defendants. A Fifth Circuit approach that infers bad faith mechanically from knowledge and theoretical incentive risks procedural unfairness, produces harsh practical consequences for creditors and debtors alike, and conflicts with New Hampshire’s insistence on a holistic inquiry into the equities, including intent. Courts may still estop in appropriate cases, but only after a totality-of-the-circumstances assessment that genuinely evaluates bad faith and the bankruptcy court’s reliance and remedial alternatives.
